title: POC Weekly - Redwood Private VPC Pilot Sync
summary: Weekly pilot sync for Redwood Private VPC deployment. Covered network routing / egress IPs, upgrade path for runtime image, observed latency regressions on long-context prompts, and next steps for benchmark runs and security paperwork. Action items assigned for upgrade runbook, bench logs, and egress IP confirmation.
topics: Egress IPs / NAT and firewall rules
KV cache behavior and prefix caching
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll keep this to 45, quick status. um, Aisha, how's your end for the network changes?
[00:22] Aisha Khan: Hey Maya, yeah so we applied the route tables last night but we're still seeing some failures to the control plane endpoint from the private subnets. we think it's the NAT config, Tom's looking into it.
[00:40] Tom Burke: yeah i rechecked security groups earlier, they allow 443 out, but the egress is hitting a proxy and it's stripping the client cert. so calls fail intermittently.
[01:05] Liam Chen: okay that matches what we saw — the agent in the private deployment relies on mutual TLS to the control plane for heartbeat and metrics. if the proxy strips the cert we fall back to the ephemeral handshake which times out.
[01:26] Priya Rao: so is the workaround to bypass the proxy for that control plane endpoint?
[01:35] Carlos Rivera: yes, either bypass or pass through client certs. we recommended adding a route for the redwood control IPs to a NAT gateway that preserves the TLS. i'll drop the exact CIDR in the slack thread.
[01:55] Evan Li: also can we get the egress IPs? our firewall policy needs to allow them as a static list.
[02:03] Maya Patel: yeah, i'll share the egress IP set and the SAML SSO callback IPs. note: if you choose private deployment with VPC egress, the IPs depend on whether you use our managed NAT or your NAT.
[02:24] Aisha Khan: noted, we'll prefer to use our NAT so we can pin the egress. Tom, can you confirm the outbound IPs by EOD?
[02:33] Tom Burke: yes, i'll confirm today.
[02:38] Liam Chen: moving to the runtime upgrade — we rolled v1.9 to the canary pool on Friday, the image includes improved KV cache eviction and attention kernel fixes. for most payloads it's a 4-8% latency win but some long-context prompts saw a regression.
[03:02] Priya Rao: we saw that in our load tests — anything above 4k tokens spiked to 400–450ms more per request on the canary.
[03:15] Carlos Rivera: right, that's the regression we were hunting. initial root cause looks like a suboptimal attention kernel chosen for the sequence length distribution in your workload. our runtime selects kernels at startup based on perf heuristics; in canary we forced a fallback that wasn't ideal.
[03:40] Aisha Khan: can you force the previous kernel until you patch? we need stable latency for user-facing pipelines.
[03:48] Liam Chen: yes, we can pin the kernel per node group. it's a config change in the runtime manifest. maya, i'll include the snippet in the runbook.
[04:02] Maya Patel: perfect. next — prefix/KV caching. we observed cache hits drop during burst tests, which explains some of the cost/latency variance. Tom, you mentioned your traffic pattern has many short unique prefixes?
[04:18] Tom Burke: yeah our bot sends distinct session prompts per user with little overlap, so prefix caching less effective. but we do have reuse at the user level for defaults.
[04:28] Carlos Rivera: for that pattern we recommend increasing the cache size and enabling per-tenant request fingerprinting so cold-starts are reduced. that will raise memory slightly but improves p99.
[04:44] Priya Rao: memory is constrained on our nodes; what's the tradeoff?
[04:50] Liam Chen: increasing the cache by 25% gave us a 12% p99 improvement in bench on similar workloads. the memory bump was about 6% on GPU for kv structures. we can also try a hybrid approach: keep cache smaller and use a local LRU for session-level reuse.
[05:10] Aisha Khan: sounds good. can we see the bench numbers?
[05:14] Maya Patel: yes, we'll upload the raw bench logs to the shared drive after the call.
[05:20] Tom Burke: quick question on KMS — we configured AWS KMS but the runtime can't decrypt model keys during boot on some nodes.
[05:30] Liam Chen: did you enable the instance profile to allow kms:Decrypt? sometimes the role doesn't assume properly on spot-like instances.
[05:38] Evan Li: i checked perms, they look fine. there were a couple nodes with clock skew which made the KMS signatures fail. we resolved that and a few decrypted.
[05:51] Carlos Rivera: yep time sync is surprisingly common root cause. we pushed an NTP fix in the bootstrap.
[06:00] Priya Rao: okay that explains it.
[06:05] Maya Patel: next, benchmarks — last week's benchmark run (v1.8 baseline) vs canary v1.9, we'll re-run with kernel pin and larger cache to isolate variables. Liam, can you own the re-run?
[06:18] Liam Chen: i can. plan to run two test matrices: mixed short/long prompts plus an all-long prompt matrix. expect ~3 hours to complete per matrix.
[06:29] Priya Rao: when can that start?
[06:31] Liam Chen: earliest is tonight after your maintenance window; otherwise tomorrow morning.
[06:36] Tom Burke: we prefer tonight.
[06:38] Liam Chen: okay i'll kick it tonight and post results by 7am PT tomorrow.
[06:45] Maya Patel: great. security paperwork — Evan, you said you needed SOC 2 and network diagrams?
[06:52] Evan Li: yes, also encryption at rest details, KMS key rotation policy, and audit log retention period.
[06:59] Maya Patel: i'll send the compliance pack and the network diagram link. note that audit logs are available both from the control plane and from the local agent; retention depends on plan.
[07:13] Aisha Khan: do you have an SLA for private deployments?
[07:17] Maya Patel: for private we offer an SLA as an add-on with uptime and latency SLOs; for pilots we usually don't include the full SLA but we can outline the contract terms for review.
[07:29] Carlos Rivera: also mentioning, for canaries we recommend gradual rollout with automatic fallback to a pinned model variant if perf regresses. that's configurable in the route policy.
[07:41] Tom Burke: how do we control fallbacks — is that per endpoint?
[07:45] Liam Chen: yes per route. you define the primary model, fallback model, and the policy (latency threshold or error rate). it's in the manifest or via the console.
[07:58] Priya Rao: one more on observability — we're missing token-level latency for batched requests in our current traces.
[08:06] Carlos Rivera: we can enable deeper tracing but it has overhead. for bench runs we'll enable full tracing for 10% sample to capture token-level behavior.
[08:18] Maya Patel: okay great. let's do a quick recap of action items.
[08:24] Maya Patel: Tom to confirm egress IPs by EOD; Liam to run bench tonight and share results by 07:00 PT tomorrow; Liam to provide kernel-pin config snippet; Maya to share egress IP list and compliance pack; Carlos to post cache tuning recommendations; Evan to confirm KMS rotation policy doc needed fields.
[08:45] Tom Burke: confirmed.
[08:47] Evan Li: i'll email the policy requirements.
[08:52] Priya Rao: can we schedule an extended SE run next Tuesday to deep dive into long-context perf?
[08:58] Liam Chen: yes we have a 90-minute slot available Tuesday 2pm PT, i'll send calendar invite.
[09:06] Maya Patel: excellent. any final Qs?
[09:09] Aisha Khan: none from me. thanks team.
[09:12] Maya Patel: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in slack and with the artifacts. bye.
